title: DSCR Loans: Financing Rentals Based on the Property's Income
description: DSCR loans qualify real estate investors on a rental's income instead of personal income. Learn how the ratio works and when this loan type makes sense.
image_alt: A brown and white residential building under a clear sky

faq.a: Debt service coverage ratio. For rental loans, it compares a property's rental income to its monthly housing expense.

faq.q: Do DSCR loans require tax returns?
faq.a: Generally no. Qualification focuses on the property's income, your credit, down payment, and reserves rather than personal income documentation.

faq.q: Can I use a DSCR loan for my primary residence?
faq.a: No. DSCR loans are designed for investment properties, not homes you'll live in.

body_html:
For real estate investors, traditional mortgage underwriting can become a bottleneck. Every additional rental adds complexity to your tax returns, and personal debt-to-income limits eventually cap how many properties you can finance. DSCR loans take a different approach: they qualify the property instead of you.

What DSCR means

DSCR stands for debt service coverage ratio. In residential lending, it compares a property's monthly rental income to its monthly housing expense: principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and any HOA dues.

A ratio above 1.0 means the rent covers the expense. Below 1.0 means it doesn't fully cover it. Each lender sets the minimum ratio it accepts, and stronger ratios generally earn better pricing. Some programs even allow ratios below 1.0 with larger down payments or reserves.

How rental income is determined

  • Existing lease: For a property that's already rented, the lease amount is often used, sometimes compared to market rent.
  • Market rent estimate: For a vacant or newly purchased property, the appraiser provides a rent schedule estimating market rent.
  • Short-term rentals: Some lenders accept short-term rental income based on history or market data, with their own rules.

DSCR vs. conventional investment loans

Conventional investment loanDSCR loan
Qualifies onYour personal income and DTIThe property's rental income
Tax returnsRequiredGenerally not required
PricingUsually lowerUsually higher
Vesting in an LLCTypically personal nameOften allowed
Scaling a portfolioLimited by DTI and property countMore flexible

Who DSCR loans fit

  • Investors with several properties whose tax returns show depreciation-heavy income
  • Self-employed investors who would rather not qualify with personal income
  • Buyers holding property in an LLC
  • Investors who want to move quickly without full personal income documentation

Trade-offs to weigh

DSCR loans are non-QM, so pricing is typically higher than conventional, and down payment and reserve expectations are larger. Many carry prepayment penalties, which can make sense for long-term holds but matter if you plan to sell or refinance soon. Always ask about the prepayment structure before you commit.

It's also worth running a conventional option first. If your personal income comfortably supports the purchase, a conventional loan may cost less.

Preparing for a DSCR purchase

  1. Estimate realistic rent using comparable listings, not best-case numbers
  2. Get insurance quotes early; landlord policies vary widely
  3. Plan your reserves for vacancy and repairs, not just for the lender
  4. Decide on vesting, personal or LLC, with your attorney or tax advisor

Running the numbers on a rental

Before you fall in love with a property, run a simple coverage check yourself. Start with a realistic monthly rent, based on comparable rentals rather than the most optimistic listing. Then estimate the full monthly housing expense: principal and interest, property taxes, landlord insurance, and HOA dues if any.

Divide the rent by the expense. If the result is comfortably above 1.0, the property likely pays its own way at the loan level. If it's close to or below 1.0, consider a larger down payment, a different price point, or a different property. Remember that the lender's ratio doesn't include vacancy, maintenance, property management, or capital repairs. Your own analysis should.

Short-term rentals and local rules

Southern California cities regulate short-term rentals very differently, and some prohibit them in certain zones altogether. If your plan depends on short-term rental income, confirm local rules and permit requirements before you buy. Lenders that accept short-term rental income may also ask for operating history or third-party market data. A property that only works as a short-term rental carries more regulatory risk than one that also works as a long-term lease.

  • Check the city's current short-term rental ordinance and permit status
  • Review HOA rules, which can prohibit short-term rentals even where the city allows them
  • Run the numbers both ways, short-term and long-term, before deciding

The takeaway

DSCR loans let a good rental qualify on its own merits. They're a powerful tool for growing a portfolio, especially when your tax returns undersell your situation. Compare them honestly against conventional options and read the prepayment terms closely. Investors whose income is mostly self-employment may also want to look at bank statement loans for a primary residence.
